The Good Samaritan
sa-MAIR-i-tan
noun phrase
From Greek plesion, “neighbour,” the parable our Lord spake to answer the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?

Biblical Definition

A certain lawyer stood up and tempted Christ, saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? (Luk 10:25); and being pointed to the law, he asked, willing to justify himself, Who is my neighbour? In answer the Lord told of a man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead (Luk 10:30). A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side; but a certain Samaritan, when he saw him, had compassion on him, bound up his wounds, set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him (Luk 10:34). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s exposition of the second great commandment, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, which the lawyer would have narrowed to his own kind. Christ widens the neighbour to whomsoever I may help, and bids him, Go, and do thou likewise (Luk 10:37). Yet the parable was framed for a man seeking to be justified by doing; and the law’s full demand of a perfect, unceasing, self-spending love is a height no fallen man attains. So the Scripture teaches that the law, which saith, This do, and thou shalt live (Luk 10:28), drives the convicted sinner from his own works to the grace he cannot earn, and to Christ, the true Neighbour, who found us half dead and bound up our wounds.

Webster 1828 Definition

The parable of the Samaritan who showed mercy to the wounded stranger, teaching the breadth of neighbour-love.

THE GOOD SAMARITAN, the parable answering the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?

A man going to Jericho fell among thieves and was left half dead.

A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side.

A Samaritan had compassion, bound his wounds, and cared for him.

Our Lord bids the hearer, Go, and do thou likewise.

Key Scripture

Luk 10:27 — "And he answering said, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself."

Luk 10:30 — "And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead."

Luk 10:33 — "But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,"

Luk 10:37 — "And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise."

Modern Corruption

The social-gospel reading detaches the parable from the lawyer’s question and the law’s demand, making it mere humanitarian works-righteousness.

expand to see more

This parable has suffered a real and widespread corruption in the progressive social gospel, which lifts it out of its frame and makes of it a bare lesson in humanitarian benevolence. The lawyer’s opening question, what shall I do to inherit eternal life, and our Lord’s closing word, this do, and thou shalt live, are quietly dropped; and the parable is preached as if good works of mercy were themselves the path to acceptance with God.

The dictionary names this for what it is: works-righteousness wearing the dress of compassion. Christ did not tell the parable to teach that men are saved by deeds of kindness, but to expose a self-justifying heart that would narrow the law’s demand to a manageable size. The law requires a love perfect, ceaseless, and whole, and by that standard the priest, the Levite, and the lawyer alike stand condemned, as do we. The full weight of this do, and thou shalt live is meant to break the sinner’s confidence in his own doing and drive him to the grace he cannot earn. So the parable is no charter for a social-gospel humanitarianism, but a tutor unto Christ, the true Neighbour, who had compassion on us when we lay half dead, and bound up our wounds at the cost of His own blood.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “neighbour,” the parable widens neighbour-love and drives the self-justifier to grace.

The Good Samaritan — from Greek plesion, “neighbour.”

It answers the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?

A Samaritan shows mercy where priest and Levite passed by.

It expounds the second great commandment of neighbour-love.

Its law-demand drives the sinner to the grace he cannot earn.

Usage

"Like the Samaritan, the believer is bound to show mercy to whomsoever he may help."

"He that shewed mercy on him. Go, and do thou likewise."

"The law’s This do, and thou shalt live drives the sinner from his works to Christ."
